title: Naegleria fowleri: Portrait of a Cerebral Killer
case_prompt:
A previously healthy 10-month-old girl from the Mekong Delta presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fevers, frequent nonbloody vomiting, and progressive lethargy. There was no history of trauma, sick contacts, or known freshwater exposure. Antenatal and postnatal courses were unremarkable. On arrival, she received empirical ceftriaxone for presumed sepsis.

Within 8 hours, she developed multiple generalized seizures and a decreased level of consciousness (U on the AVPU scale), requiring intubation. After intubation, she progressed to a deep coma without response to stimuli. She was managed in the intensive care unit with mechanical ventilation, intravenous meropenem and vancomycin, intracranial pressure control (mannitol and hypertonic saline), and emergency external ventricular drainage.

Brain ultrasound and computed tomography scan showed acute hydrocephalus. Laboratory studies revealed a C-reactive protein level of 151 mg/L. Urinalysis and urine cultures were negative. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. 

Cerebrospinal fluid obtained at presentation was turbid yellow, with 4,032 white cells/mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), lactate 11.8 mmol/L, protein 6.9 g/L, and normal plasma glucose. Serial CSF and blood bacterial microscopy and cultures were negative. PCR assays for herpes simplex virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Autoimmune markers (antibody and complement levels) and HIV testing were normal or negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Broad bacterial or viral infections such as viral gastroenteritis, urinary tract infection, and sepsis were initially considered because of nonspecific symptoms — “viral gastroenteritis, urinary tract infection and sepsis of unknown origin can all present with nonspecific symptoms, such as vomiting and lethargy, without localized signs.”  
2. A surgical cause such as intussusception was contemplated despite low likelihood given age and presentation — “Although less likely, intussusception should also be considered as a possible surgical cause for this child presentation, as it can present with vomiting and lethargy, and sometimes fever, especially in this child’s age group.”  
3. Bacterial meningitis was high on the differential due to neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis and elevated protein, but was excluded by negative CSF and blood cultures — “This marked neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis is characteristic of bacterial meningitis, but can also occur in other severe infections or inflammatory conditions like amebic meningoencephalitis.”; “Subsequent blood and CSF bacterial microscopy and culture were negative.”  
4. Common viral and mycobacterial encephalitides (herpes simplex virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) were excluded by negative molecular tests — “All other diagnostic tests, for common encephalitis pathogens in Vietnam such as herpes simplex virus, Japanese encephalitis virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, were also negative.”  
5. Noninfectious inflammatory processes and HIV were considered but ruled out by normal autoimmune markers and negative HIV testing — “Auto-immune indicators, such as antibody, and complement levels were all within normal limits. The anti-HIV result was also negative.”
